notes.summary: Proved full-family classical positivity for every usc obstacle on curve bases with perfected bijective normalization, multiplied by smooth geometrically connected projective factors, and on analytic projective bundles over those curves. Global competitor descent, relative boundary and all scalar curve tests are covered. This is a sufficient geometric sector, not the sharp higher-dimensional classification.
notes.detailedSummary: The checked GJR definitions identify the exact LFS/semipositive-real-PL union with the full semipositive real-PL class. Every competitor is constant on a connected compact boundaryless projective fiber. A finite extension constructed from an algebraic closed point supplies an analytic section, and published finite real-PL and semipositivity descent recovers a global base competitor without requiring a ground-field point. Projective bundles instead use local sections and ordinary sheaf gluing. Smoothness proves ordinary openness of projection, giving exact fiber-infimum obstacle reduction and regularization compatibility. A fresh curve-family argument uses anchored finite maxima on the interior of the perfected normalization, followed by boundary extension and finite/scalar descent. Concrete normal analytic domains and geometrically unibranch nonnormal cusp products are verified. No positivity theorem for arbitrary normal higher-dimensional affinoids or sharp necessary-and-sufficient classification follows.
notes.text:
This note proves a sufficient sector for P03.1, using checked published foundations and complete new applications. Let \(K\) be complete and nontrivially valued. Spaces carrying PL functions are good, separated and strictly analytic. Write \(\operatorname{SP}_{\mathbb R}(W)\) for finite semipositive real-PL functions, and let \(P_Wf\) be the raw envelope over the exact locally Fubini–Study/semipositive-real-PL union.

The primary definitions matter. Gubler–Jell–Rabinoff, arXiv:2111.05741, Definition 5.1 makes real-PL functions finite and continuous. Definitions 7.2 and 7.8 define semipositivity by nef residues and LFS by semiample residues. Therefore LFS is already a subclass of semipositive real PL, and the literal union is exactly \(\mathcal E_W(f)=\{h\in\operatorname{SP}_{\mathbb R}(W):h\le f\}\). Gubler–Rabinoff, arXiv:2506.13548v2, Theorem 4.3 identifies this class with real-PL functions that are classically psh. Its Definition 4.1 requires curve pullbacks after every analytic field extension. These statements apply over a nontrivially valued field on good strict spaces.

The precise local LFS presentation used below is GJR 7.9: nonnegative combinations of maxima of negative logs of analytic units, with the real-PL requirement. In particular, for analytic \(F_1,\ldots,F_r\), \(c\in K^\times\), and integer \(n\ge1\),
\[H=\frac1n\log\max\{|c|,|F_1|,\ldots,|F_r|\}\]
is rational PL and LFS. Near any point, discard functions vanishing there because their norms become smaller than \(|c|\); retained functions become units. Rational dominance domains give a strict G-cover on which \(H\) is one unit log divided by \(n\). On the ordinary open neighborhood its presentation is \(n^{-1}\max(-\log|c^{-1}|,-\log|F_j^{-1}|)\), with positive coefficient and units. Constants are also LFS. This argument does not assume closure of arbitrary real-PL functions under maxima.

We first prove the curve input. Let \(C\) be a reduced separated strict analytic curve. In positive characteristic let \(K^{\mathrm p}=\widehat{K^{1/p^\infty}}\); otherwise let \(K^{\mathrm p}=K\). Assume normalization of \((C_{K^{\mathrm p}})_{\mathrm{red}}\) is bijective on Berkovich points. The regularized supremum of every nonempty locally upper-bounded family of finite continuous classically psh functions on \(C\) is classically psh, with absolute boundary allowed.

Here is the proof. GR Lemmas 3.7–3.9 say that perfected scalar extension and reduction are homeomorphisms, that normalization is finite and a topological quotient, and that the normalized curve over the perfect field is rig-smooth. The assumed bijectivity makes normalization a homeomorphism. Their composite \(t:\widetilde C\to C\) is thus a homeomorphism, and regularization commutes with pullback along it. All family members pull back to classically psh functions. Choose one finite continuous member \(h_0\), and direct finite subsets containing it by inclusion. Their finite maxima are continuous psh functions with the same supremum as the original family. They need not be PL competitors, and no such assertion is needed. On every sufficiently small neighborhood they are bounded above uniformly and bounded below by \(h_0\circ t\).

On \(\operatorname{Int}(\widetilde C)\), a smooth strict curve, Thuillier's thesis, Proposition 3.1.8(iii), makes the usc regularized supremum subharmonic. The original PDF says increasing and locally bounded; the anchored maxima satisfy both upper and lower local bounds. GR 3.4.1 identifies this with its extended subharmonic convention. The function is usc on the whole normalized curve, so GR Proposition 3.5(3) extends subharmonicity across absolute boundary. Descend through normalization and reduction by finite-surjective descent, Proposition 3.5(8), then through perfected scalar extension by Proposition 3.5(7). The descended function is the original regularized supremum. On a curve, GR 4.1.2 identifies subharmonicity with classical pshness. These propositions use the all-extension definitions, so further analytic scalar extensions are included. The empty family gives identically \(-\infty\), permitted by Definition 3.4. No supplied book curve theorem is used.

Now let \(B\) be any good separated strict base and let \(Y\) be a nonempty smooth geometrically connected projective \(K\)-scheme. Put \(X=B\times_KY^{\mathrm{an}}\) and let \(p:X\to B\). We prove the exact global bijection
\[p^*:\operatorname{SP}_{\mathbb R}(B)\xrightarrow{\sim}\operatorname{SP}_{\mathbb R}(X).\]
Berkovich, IHÉS 78 (1993), Propositions 2.6.1, 2.6.9 and 3.5.8 establish boundaryless analytification, projective properness and smoothness; Proposition 3.5.2 preserves smoothness under base change. Thus \(p\) is proper and smooth, and Corollary 3.7.4 makes it an ordinary open map, including above absolute-boundary base points. Its fiber at \(x\) is \((Y_{\mathcal H(x)})^{\mathrm{an}}\), nonempty, compact and boundaryless over \(\mathcal H(x)\).

The fiber is connected, as follows from an exact checked primary statement. Berkovich Theorem 7.1.1 compares compactly supported étale cohomology for a compactifiable scheme and its analytification. Apply degree zero to the proper connected scheme \(Y_{\mathcal H(x)}\) and a finite constant sheaf \(\mathbb Z/\ell\mathbb Z\). Properness identifies compactly supported and ordinary sections, whose group downstairs is \(\mathbb Z/\ell\mathbb Z\). A nontrivial clopen partition of the analytic fiber would give a nonconstant section upstairs, contradicting the comparison. Hence the fiber is connected.

For any \(h\in\operatorname{SP}_{\mathbb R}(X)\), pull back to \(X_{\mathcal H(x)}\) and restrict along the analytic fiber morphism. GR Proposition 4.2 makes this restriction classically psh. Its finite continuous maximum exists on the compact fiber. The maximum set is nonempty and closed; the fiber is boundaryless, so GR Theorem 6.1 makes it open. Connectedness forces constancy. Thus \(h=g\circ p\) for a unique finite function \(g\). A proper map between these locally compact Hausdorff spaces is closed: restrict a closed set to inverse images of compact base neighborhoods and use compactness. Consequently \(p\) is a quotient and \(g\) is continuous.

It remains to recover an actual global base competitor. Choose an algebraic closed point of \(Y\) in a nonempty affine chart. Zariski's lemma gives a finite residue extension \(M/K\), complete for the extended valuation, and an \(M\)-point of \(Y_M\). This constructs an analytic section \(\sigma_M:B_M\to X_M\). Then
\[g\circ\pi_{M/K}=h_M\circ\sigma_M\in\operatorname{SP}_{\mathbb R}(B_M).\]
GJR Corollary 5.12, with divisible coefficient group \(\mathbb R\), descends real-PLness along this finite scalar extension. Proposition 7.6(2') descends semipositivity. Thus \(g\) is a global member on \(B\). Conversely pullback preserves the class by GJR Lemma 5.4 and Proposition 7.6. This proves the bijection without a ground-field rational point, Galois action, section palette or globalization assumption.

For any usc obstacle \(f\) on \(X\), define \(F(x)=\inf_{p(y)=x}f(y)\). This takes values in \(\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}\), and is usc because \(\{F<a\}=p(\{f<a\})\) is open. The competitor bijection gives
\[\mathcal E_X(f)=p^*\mathcal E_B(F),\qquad P_Xf=(P_BF)\circ p.\]
These identities include empty families. For a continuous open surjection and any locally upper-bounded raw function \(a\),
\[(a\circ p)^*=a^*\circ p.\]
One inequality follows by pulling back base neighborhoods. For the other, every neighborhood \(W\ni y\) has open image containing \(p(y)\), and \(\sup_Wa\circ p=\sup_{p(W)}a\ge a^*(p(y))\). Hence
\[(P_Xf)^*=(P_BF)^*\circ p.\]
Every bound and identity concerns the complete competitor family.

The same conclusions hold for analytic projective bundles \(p:\mathbb P(\mathcal V)\to B\), where \(\mathcal V\) is an ordinary locally free analytic vector bundle of constant rank at least two. Local trivializations are products with projective space and prove properness, smoothness, openness and connected boundaryless fibers. Fiber constancy again gives \(h=g\circ p\). Restriction along a coordinate section on each trivializing base open proves that \(g\) is semipositive real PL there. GJR's ordinary sheaf properties glue these agreeing restrictions to one global competitor. No global section is assumed.

Take \(B=C\) satisfying the proved curve hypothesis. For a nonempty family the base competitors are finite continuous psh functions locally upper bounded by the usc \(F\). The curve lemma makes \(u_C=(P_CF)^*\) classically psh. The identities above prove \((P_Xf)^*=u_C\circ p\). Explicitly, for every analytic extension \(K'/K\) and every curve morphism \(\gamma:D\to X_{K'}\), its pullback is
\[u_C\circ\pi_{C,K'/K}\circ p_{K'}\circ\gamma,\]
which is subharmonic by the classical definition for \(u_C\). This verifies all scalar curve tests without assuming openness of arbitrary scalar projections or identifying upstairs competitor families. The obstacle fiber infimum itself does commute with scalar extension: every ground fiber point has a lift over any chosen scalar base point, using the nonempty spectrum of \(\mathcal H(y)\widehat\otimes_{\mathcal H(x)}\mathcal H(x')\), the checked fiber-product foundation in GR 2.8. Thus the sets of obstacle values in those fibers agree. This does not prove full competitor base-change compatibility.

Relative boundary is included. Projection is boundaryless relative to the separated good curve, so the GR 2.11 boundary formula gives \(\partial X=p^{-1}(\partial C)\). The curve proof handled base boundary before descent. Projective fiber constancy used boundarylessness over its own completed residue field even above such base points.

These hypotheses have concrete normal realizations. Take \(C\) to be a good strict analytic domain in a smooth separated algebraic curve and \(Y\) as above. The product is an analytic domain in a smooth algebraic product. Berkovich Corollaries 2.2.7–2.2.8 give regular analytic local rings and regular affinoid domains, hence normality. The same applies after extension, so the curve normalization hypothesis holds. Projective bundles are normal by their local product charts. Closed strict discs and annuli are included, with absolute boundary allowed; the product dimension is \(1+\dim Y\).

There are actual nonnormal geometrically unibranch examples. Over \(\mathbb Q_3\), let \(C=\mathcal M(K\langle u,v\rangle/(v^2-u^3))\). Its normalization is \(K\langle T\rangle\), with \(u=T^2,v=T^3\). The expansion \(a(u)+vb(u)\) maps injectively to disjoint even and odd powers; the image consists of series with no linear \(T\)-coefficient. Adjoining integral \(T\), with \(T=v/u\) in the fraction field, gives the normal Tate algebra finitely. Away from the origin the map is an isomorphism; over it there is one point with the same residue field. These computations persist after every field extension. For \(C\times Y^{\mathrm{an}}\), the finite birational map from the normal disc product is normalization. At a point of the cusp section its fiber algebra is \(H[T]/(T^2,T^3)\), with a single underlying point after every residue extension. Thus these products are geometrically unibranch and nonnormal, and the theorem covers every noninvariant usc obstacle on them.

Limitations: this does not prove the sharp normal/geometrically-unibranch higher-dimensional classification, arbitrary normal affinoid positivity, continuity, or CLD-stage positivity. It establishes the displayed actual geometric sectors only.

notes.summary: Explicit full-family continuous-obstacle failures on split branches and codimension-two point pinchings, including a single irreducible bidisc with two rational points identified. Its strict affinoid algebra, seminormal analytic germs and normality off one codimension-two point are proved; genuine global rational LFS minorants force a closed-disc failure.
notes.detailedSummary: For two closed polydiscs glued at their origins, the full raw envelope is computed exactly: zero on one punctured component and a negative constant on the other including the origin. Regularization raises the origin and fails a disc test. An additional irreducible example uses the subalgebra of the bidisc consisting of functions with equal values at two rational points. A bounded algebra decomposition proves affinoidness and finite normalization; its conductor and analytic germ kernel prove the stated geometry and seminormality. A continuous obstacle descends from the normalization, while polynomials vanishing at both identified points give global rational LFS minorants. The bad disc bounds every competitor at the pinched point, and the good disc forces regularization to exceed that bound. These independently proved examples establish insufficiency of seminormality and codimension-one normality; they do not classify the geometrically unibranch range.
notes.text:
Use the exact competitor identification, rational LFS presentation and published classical maximum principles checked in n1. Fix \(0<|\varpi|<1\), put \(\rho=|\varpi|\), and \(a=-\log\rho>0\).

First, for \(d\ge1\), define
\[A_d=K\langle X_1,\ldots,X_d,Y_1,\ldots,Y_d\rangle/(X_iY_j),\qquad W_d=\mathcal M(A_d).\]
There is an explicit ring identity
\[A_d=K\langle X_1,\ldots,X_d\rangle\times_KK\langle Y_1,\ldots,Y_d\rangle,\]
with evaluations at the origins. Modulo the cross terms a series has one common constant, an \(X\)-series without constant term and a \(Y\)-series without constant term. Thus the space is reduced, strict and pure of dimension \(d\). Its normalization is the product of the two normal Tate algebras, finite by adjoining the idempotent \((1,0)\). Outside the common origin \(o\), a nonzero coordinate removes the other component, so normalization is an isomorphism and the space is normal.

It is seminormal. For an element of the total fraction ring whose square and cube belong to \(A_d\), normality puts its two coordinates in the respective Tate algebras. Their constant terms \(\alpha,\beta\) satisfy \(\alpha^2=\beta^2\) and \(\alpha^3=\beta^3\), hence \(\alpha=\beta\), so the element belongs to \(A_d\). More directly, a subintegral intermediate extension in the normalization has a unique prime over \(o\) with residue field \(K\). Its two evaluations into \(K\) must agree, so all its elements have equal constant terms and it equals \(A_d\). The same argument works for analytic germs: at \(o\) they are the fiber product of the two regular polydisc germ rings over their residue field \(K\), obtained by taking arbitrarily small polydisc neighborhoods. Elsewhere the germs are normal. For \(d=2\), this gives a seminormal space normal away from a codimension-two point.

Set
\[f=-a\max_j|Y_j|,\qquad h_n=\frac1n\log\max\{\rho^n,|X_1|,\ldots,|X_d|\}.\]
The obstacle is finite continuous. The local presentation in n1 proves that each \(h_n\) is a global rational LFS function. On the \(X\)-component it is at most zero, equal to the obstacle bound; on the \(Y\)-component it equals \(-a\le f\). The constant \(-a\) is another competitor.

For any competitor in the full union, its restriction to the \(Y\)-polydisc is classically psh. The Gauss norm dominates every Tate-series evaluation and is multiplicative, so the polydisc has a singleton Shilov boundary. There the obstacle equals \(-a\). The classical affinoid maximum principle therefore bounds every competitor by \(-a\) throughout that component, including \(o\). On the punctured \(X\)-component at least one coordinate has positive norm, and \(h_n\) increases to zero. Thus the exact full raw envelope is zero on that punctured component and \(-a\) on the entire \(Y\)-component including \(o\).

Regularization raises \(o\) to zero, because punctured \(X\)-points approach it and the continuous obstacle is zero there. Every other \(Y\)-point has a neighborhood avoiding the \(X\)-component, so its regularized value remains \(-a\). Pullback along the closed-disc axis \(Y_1=T\), other coordinates zero, has value zero at its origin and \(-a\) at its singleton Shilov point. It violates the maximum principle and is not classically psh. This proves split failure for every \(d\). The exact descent theorem in n1, which allowed an arbitrary base, also transfers this example to \(W_d\times Y^{\mathrm{an}}\) for the projective factors there. A finite extension supplying a point of the factor gives the same axis as a scalar curve test.

The codimension-two obstruction also has an irreducible realization. Let
\[B=K\langle T,Z\rangle,\quad P=(0,0),\quad Q=(1,0),\quad A=\{g\in B:g(P)=g(Q)\},\quad W=\mathcal M(A).\]
We prove affinoidness rather than assume that this pinching is realizable. Put \(U=T(T-1)\), \(R_0=K\langle U,Z\rangle\). Then
\[B=R_0\oplus TR_0,\qquad A=R_0\oplus T(U,Z)R_0.\]
For the first decomposition, reduce powers by \(T^2=T+U\). If \(T^m=a_m(U)+Tc_m(U)\), the recurrence is \((a_{m+1},c_{m+1})=(Uc_m,a_m+c_m)\), starting at \((1,0)\). These integer-coefficient polynomials have Gauss norms at most one, so reduction of a convergent Tate series gives convergent \(a,c\in R_0\), bounded by its norm. Substitution \(U=T(T-1)\) embeds \(R_0\) isometrically: scale a coefficient of maximal norm to one and reduce; a nonzero polynomial in \(U,Z\) remains nonzero under \(U=T^2-T\). Uniqueness follows by substituting \(1-T\) and subtracting, obtaining \((2T-1)c(U,Z)=0\) in the domain \(B\). This also works in characteristic two.

The two evaluation values of \(a+Tc\) differ by \(c(0,0)\), proving the formula for \(A\). It is generated over \(R_0\) by \(TU,TZ\) and is a finite module. The bounded map \(K\langle U,Z,V,R\rangle\to B\), \(V=TU,R=TZ\), has image exactly \(A\): split the monomials of \(c\in(U,Z)\) to write \(c=Uc_1+Zc_2\), then \(a+Tc=a+Vc_1+Rc_2\). These operations give a bounded linear right inverse. Hence the quotient norm and closed subspace norm are equivalent, and \(A\) is an actual strict affinoid quotient. It is an integral domain because it embeds in \(B\).

Adjoining \(T\), integral by \(T^2-T-U=0\), gives \(B\); it is birational because \(T=(TU)/U\) in the fraction field. Since \(B\) is normal, \(\nu:\mathcal M(B)\to W\) is finite normalization. Its conductor is \(I=(U,Z)B\): these functions vanish at \(P,Q\), whereas multiplication by \(T\) and \(1-T\) shows that every conductor element must vanish at both. Moreover
\[B/I=K\times K,\qquad A/I=K.\]
Exactly \(P,Q\) are identified to a rational point \(\xi\). Outside it normalization is an isomorphism. The space is irreducible of dimension two and normal away from \(\xi\), which has codimension two.

It is seminormal as an analytic space. Any integral birational extension lies in \(B\); if subintegral, its two evaluations at \(P,Q\) must agree, so it is contained in \(A\) and equals \(A\). For germs, use the exact finite-module sequence
\[0\to A\to B\xrightarrow{g\mapsto g(Q)-g(P)}K_\xi\to0.\]
The checked finite-module/coherent-sheaf correspondence on good affinoids, Berkovich 1.3 and Proposition 1.3.4, identifies the germ kernel with the equal-residue fiber product of the normal bidisc germs at \(P,Q\). The finite pushforward stalk has those two factors: properness allows inverse images of sufficiently small base neighborhoods to lie in any prescribed disjoint neighborhoods of the two fiber points. The same equal-evaluation argument rules out a proper subintegral germ extension. Other germs are normal.

Define a continuous function on \([0,1]\) by
\[\phi(r)=\begin{cases}-ar/\rho&0\le r\le\rho,\\ \log r&\rho\le r\le1.\end{cases}\]
The formulas agree at \(\rho\), and \(\phi(0)=\phi(1)=0\). On normalization let \(\widetilde f=\phi(|T-1|)\). Its values at \(P,Q\) both equal zero, so it descends through the finite closed quotient to a finite continuous obstacle \(f\) on \(W\).

The polynomials \(F_n=T(T-1)^n\) belong to \(A\), since they vanish at both identified points. Hence
\[h_n=\frac1n\log\max\{\rho^n,|F_n|\}\]
are genuine global rational LFS functions on \(W\). On normalization, \(|T|\le1\), giving
\[h_n\circ\nu\le\max\{-a,\log|T-1|\}\le\phi(|T-1|)=f\circ\nu.\]
The second inequality is \(-a\le-ar/\rho\) for \(r\le\rho\), and equality for \(r\ge\rho\). Thus they and the constant \(-a\) are full-family minorants.

The bad closed disc \((T,Z)=(1+\varpi S,0)\), composed with normalization, maps its origin to \(\xi\). At its Gauss point \(|T-1|=\rho\), so \(f=-a\). Every competitor pulls back to a classically psh function on this disc; its singleton-Shilov maximum principle gives \(h(\xi)\le-a\). The baseline realizes equality, so the raw envelope at \(\xi\) is \(-a\).

On the good disc \((T,Z)=(\varpi S,0)\), every nonzero-radius point has \(|T-1|=1\), obstacle zero, and \(|F_n|=|T|>0\). The displayed minorants have supremum zero there, computing the full raw envelope at those points. They approach \(\xi\), so its regularized value is zero. At the bad disc's Gauss point regularization stays at most \(-a\), since the continuous obstacle is an usc majorant of the raw envelope. The bad disc therefore fails the Shilov maximum principle.

This is an independently constructed irreducible, seminormal strict surface normal away from one codimension-two point, with a continuous obstacle and full-family classical-psh failure. It is not asserted identical to the supplied book example, and it does not establish a counterexample within the geometrically unibranch range.

notes.summary: Constructed an explicit continuous-obstacle failure for the full competitor family on the irreducible nonsplit quadratic-node surface over \(\mathbb Q_3\). Truncated binomial polynomials give global rational LFS minorants, and a genuine quadratic-extension closed-disc test fails. Pointwise bijective curve normalization is therefore insufficient as a product-stable substitute. The original sharp classification remains unresolved.
notes.detailedSummary: The nonsplit curve is an integral strict affinoid with finite normalization \(L\langle T\rangle\), where \(L=\mathbb Q_3(\sqrt2)\); every ground-field normalization fiber is a singleton. Its product with the strict open disc is an actual reduced irreducible surface, and a quadratic-residue nodal point has two normalization lifts. A continuous cutoff obstacle lies between \(-3b\) and zero. Explicit rational LFS functions built from truncated binomial coefficients are bounded globally by zero and equal \(-3b\) wherever the obstacle is negative, so they are global minorants. The plus-branch disc bounds every full-family competitor at the node by \(-3b\); the minus branch gives raw lower bound \(-2b\) at positive radii approaching it. Regularization thus violates the plus disc's singleton-Shilov maximum principle. This proves the nonsplit necessity obstruction, not a failure on a normal or geometrically unibranch higher-dimensional domain and not a complete solution of P03.1.
notes.text:
Use the full-family identification, local rational LFS presentation and classical scalar pullback/maximum principles established and checked in n1. The necessity examples in n2 remain separate from the construction here.

Let \(K=\mathbb Q_3\), \(\rho=|3|=1/3\), \(b=-\log\rho>0\), and \(L=K(\alpha)\) with \(\alpha^2=2\). The polynomial is irreducible because 2 is nonsquare modulo 3, and \(|\alpha|=1\). Define
\[C=\mathcal M(K\langle X,Y\rangle/(X^2-2Y^2)),\quad D=\{|Z|<1\}\subset\mathbb A_K^{1,\mathrm{an}},\quad X_0=C\times_KD.\]
The surface is named \(X_0\); \(X\) is a coordinate.

The curve algebra injects into \(L\langle T\rangle\), with \(Y=T,X=\alpha T\). Reduction by the monic quadratic relation writes an element uniquely as \(a(Y)+Xc(Y)\). Its image has constant coefficient in \(K\) and arbitrary coefficients in \(L\) in positive degree: in degree \(m\ge1\) the coefficient is \(a_m+\alpha c_{m-1}\). The two \(K\)-components are independent. Thus the curve algebra is a domain. Adjoining integral \(\alpha\), which equals \(X/Y\) in the fraction field, gives the normal algebra \(L\langle T\rangle\), finitely and birationally. This is normalization.

If \(|Y|>0\), normalization is an isomorphism with inverse \(\alpha=X/Y\). Over \(X=Y=0\), its fiber is \(\mathcal M(L)\), one point. Hence every ground-field Berkovich normalization fiber on the curve is a singleton. After extension to \(L\) the curve has two branches \(X=\pm\alpha Y\). At the product point with \(X=Y=0\) and \(Z^2=18\), the completed residue field is \(L\), and the normalization fiber is \(\mathcal M(L\otimes_KL)=\mathcal M(L\times L)\), two points.

The surface is reduced, irreducible, good, separated and strict, of dimension two. For an explicit strict exhaustion of \(D\), take \(|Z|^m\le|3|\), whose algebra has the presentation \(K\langle Z,W\rangle/(Z^m-3W)\). On each such chart the surface algebra is the subalgebra of the integral polydisc algebra \(L\langle T,r^{-1}Z\rangle\) with constant coefficient in \(T\) belonging to \(K\langle r^{-1}Z\rangle\); it is a domain. The nested charts cover the open disc and their components overlap in nonempty interiors. Equivalently, the finite birational normalization is a connected normal polydisc domain over \(L\), hence irreducible. This verifies actual geometry rather than postulating a scalar orbit or abstract realization.

Define \(r=|Y|\), \(G=3X-ZY\), and
\[\eta(r)=\min\{1,\max\{0,(r-\rho)/(1-\rho)\}\},\qquad\chi(R)=\max\{0,1-R/\rho\}.\]
Set the obstacle to
\[f=\begin{cases}-3b\,\eta(r)\,\chi(|G|/(\rho r))&r>0,\\0&r=0.\end{cases}\]
It is finite continuous and lies in \([-3b,0]\). The ratio is continuous where \(r>0\); near \(r=0\), \(\eta\) vanishes on the entire region \(r\le\rho\), eliminating any continuity issue.

For \(n\ge1\), put
\[\delta=Z^2/18-1,\quad c_j=\binom{-1/2}{j},\quad P_n(t)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}c_jt^j,\]
\[A_n(Z)=(Z/3)P_n(\delta),\quad F_n=X-A_n(Z)Y,\quad h_n=\frac1n\log\max\{|3|^{3n},|3^{2n}F_n|\}.\]
These use global polynomials. The precise presentation in n1 makes each \(h_n\) a global rational LFS function, including at its zeros.

The identity \(c_j=(-1)^j\binom{2j}{j}/4^j\) proves \(|c_j|_3\le1\). On the whole surface \(|Z|<1\), \(|X|,|Y|\le1\), and \(|\delta|\le\rho^{-2}\). Consequently
\[|A_n|\le\rho^{-(2n-1)},\quad |F_n|\le\rho^{-(2n-1)},\quad |3^{2n}F_n|\le\rho,\]
so \(-3b\le h_n\le0\) globally.

We prove the stronger bound where \(f<0\). Such a point has \(r>\rho\) and \(R=|G|/(\rho r)<\rho\). In its completed residue field put \(t=X/Y\), so \(t^2=2\), \(|t|=1\), and \(w=Z/(3t)\). Then \(|w-1|=R<\rho\) and \(\delta=w^2-1\), with \(|\delta|<\rho\). The series \(B(\delta)=\sum_{j\ge0}c_j\delta^j\) converges in that complete field. Its formal binomial identity gives \((1+\delta)B(\delta)^2=1\). Both \(w\) and \(B(\delta)\) are within distance less than one of 1, so \(wB(\delta)\) is the root \(+1\), not \(-1\), of its square-one equation; here \(|2|_3=1\). Hence \(B(\delta)=w^{-1}\), and
\[|A_n-t|=|tw(P_n(\delta)-B(\delta))|\le|\delta|^n\le\rho^n.\]
Therefore \(|F_n|\le\rho^n|Y|\le\rho^n\), giving \(h_n=-3b\) wherever \(f<0\). There \(h_n\le f\); elsewhere \(f=0\) and the global bound applies. Thus all \(h_n\) are genuine global members of the full obstacle family. In particular the family is nonempty; the constant \(-3b\) is also a minorant.

Over the actual analytic extension \(L/K\), consider closed-disc morphisms
\[\gamma_\pm:\mathcal M(L\langle T\rangle)\to(X_0)_L,\qquad(X,Y,Z)=(\pm\alpha T,T,3\alpha).\]
They land in the open factor because \(|3\alpha|=\rho<1\). Their origins have the same ground-field image \(\xi\), the quadratic-residue nodal point described above.

At the plus-disc Gauss point, \(r=1,G=0\), so \(f=-3b\). Every competitor in the full union is classically psh and its scalar pullback obeys the singleton-Shilov maximum principle. Thus \(h(\xi)\le-3b\) for every competitor. The explicit minorants equal \(-3b\) there, proving the exact raw value \(s(\xi)=-3b\), where \(s=P_{X_0}f\).

On the minus disc, \(\delta=0,A_n=\alpha,F_n=-2\alpha T\). Since \(|2\alpha|=1\), at every point with \(|T|>0\),
\[h_n\circ\gamma_-=\max\{-3b,-2b+n^{-1}\log|T|\},\qquad\sup_nh_n\circ\gamma_-=-2b.\]
Positive-radius points approach the origin and project continuously to \(\xi\). Hence \(s^*(\xi)\ge-2b\). The continuous obstacle is an usc majorant of \(s\), so \(s^*\le f\); its value at the projected plus-disc Gauss point is therefore at most \(-3b\).

The pullback \(s^*\circ\pi_{L/K}\circ\gamma_+\) has origin value at least \(-2b\) and singleton Shilov value at most \(-3b\). It violates the affinoid maximum principle. Thus the full regularized envelope is not classically psh. This is a scalar curve-test counterexample with a continuous obstacle and actual global rational LFS minorants, not merely a topological defect function or an invariant-envelope calculation.

Its product with the displayed open disc fails. Pointwise normalization bijectivity is consequently not a product-stable replacement for the requested higher-dimensional geometry.
